How I Did It: Neon Cycles

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

Summer of '82, the movie came out and every kid in Portland wanted on my Tron cabinet the same afternoon. Two brothers, the Kowalskis, used to play the light cycles against each other so hard that the loser had to buy the winner a Coke from the machine by the door. I made more off that Coke machine than the cabinet some weeks. The light cycle part was everybody's favorite — simple as drawing a line, mean as a knife fight.

What the remodel changed

My '25 version let the bikes drift around on loose pixels, which meant sometimes you'd clip a wall you swore you missed. The robots put the whole arena on a proper grid this time — a hundred cells across — and every bike, mine and the computer's, moves cell by cell under the exact same rules. No cheating possible, in either direction. The bikes still look like they glide because the drawing slides them smoothly between cells, but the crash math is honest squares. And the computer riders got personalities: one tries to cut you off, one plays it safe, one's a little unhinged. Plus a boost button, because the Kowalskis would've demanded one.

The spell that did it

Rebuild Neon Cycles grid-based so it's fair — the AI and I follow identical collision rules, no fuzzy pixel checks. Trails are walls, 90-degree turns only, swipe to steer on a phone. Give me up to three AI riders with different personalities: an aggressive one that cuts across my path, a cautious one that hugs open space, and an erratic one that's random but never suicidal. Add a boost meter I hold A to burn. Make it gorgeous — glowing heads, glowing trails, a tinted arena that changes color every level.

Under the hood

  • The arena is a 100-by-72 grid of on/off cells. A bike asks "is the next cell free?" before it enters — if not, it derezzes. That one rule covers walls, your own trail, and everybody else's.
  • Bikes advance at cells-per-second scaled by the engine's fixed time step, and the drawing interpolates the head between cells so a chunky grid still looks like liquid neon.
  • When an AI needs to turn, it counts how much open floor it can reach in each direction — a little flood-fill, capped so it stays cheap — and the aggressive one subtracts points for being far from a spot projected ahead of my bike. That's the cut-off move.
  • Trails are drawn as one glowing polyline per bike (a corner point gets added only when it turns), so a long round doesn't slow the drawing down one bit.
